Existing methods primarily focus on vision-based sensors and emphasize image rendering quality while providing overly simplistic models of force and shear. Consequently, these models exhibit a large sim-to-real gap for many dexterous tasks. Here, we present HydroShear, a non-holonomic hydroelastic tactile simulator that advances the state-of-the-art by modeling: a) stick-slip transitions, b) path-dependent force and shear build up, and c) full SE(3) object-sensor interactions. HydroShear extends hydroelastic contact models using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) to track the displacements of the on-surface points of an indenter during physical interaction with the sensor membrane. Our approach generates physics-based, computationally efficient force fields from arbitrary watertight geometries while remaining agnostic to the underlying physics engine. In experiments with GelSight Minis, HydroShear more faithfully reproduces real tactile shear compared to existing methods. This fidelity enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of reinforcement learning policies across four tasks: peg insertion, bin packing, book shelving for insertion, and drawer pulling for fine gripper control under slip. Our method achieves a 93% average success rate, outperforming policies trained on tactile images (34%) and alternative shear simulation methods (58%-61%).
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: OxyGen: Unified KV Cache Management for VLA Inference under Multi-Task Parallelism
item.description: arXiv:2603.14371v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Embodied AI agents increasingly require parallel execution of multiple tasks, such as manipulation, conversation, and memory construction, from shared observations under distinct time constraints. Recent Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) support such heterogeneous outputs, yet existing inference systems incur redundant computation and resource contention when serving concurrent tasks on-device. We identify isolated KV cache management as the root cause. To address this, we propose unified KV cache management, an inference design that treats the KV cache as a first-class shared resource across tasks and control cycles. This abstraction enables two key optimizations: cross-task KV sharing eliminates redundant prefill of shared observations, while cross-frame continuous batching batches unfinished language requests from different frames and advances them within a per-frame decoding budget. We implement this design in OxyGen and evaluate $\pi_{0.5}$ on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 and Jetson AGX Thor. OxyGen achieves up to 3.7$\times$ speedup over isolated execution, delivering over 200 tokens/s language throughput and 70 Hz action frequency simultaneously on RTX 4090. We also validate the design on Xiaomi-Robotics-0 and StarVLA across different backbones and expert configurations. We further demonstrate the inference gains on a humanoid robot with on-board Jetson AGX Thor.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Understanding and Defending VLM Jailbreaks via Jailbreak-Related Representation Shift
item.description: arXiv:2603.17372v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large vision-language models (VLMs) often exhibit weakened safety alignment with the integration of the visual modality. Even when text prompts contain explicit harmful intent, adding an image can substantially increase jailbreak success rates. In this paper, we observe that VLMs can clearly distinguish benign inputs from harmful ones in their representation space. Moreover, even among harmful inputs, jailbreak samples form a distinct internal state that is separable from refusal samples. These observations suggest that jailbreaks do not arise from a failure to recognize harmful intent. Instead, the visual modality shifts representations toward a specific jailbreak state, thereby leading to a failure to trigger refusal. To quantify this transition, we identify a jailbreak direction and define the jailbreak-related shift as the component of the image-induced representation shift along this direction. Our analysis shows that the jailbreak-related shift reliably characterizes jailbreak behavior, providing a unified explanation for diverse jailbreak scenarios. Finally, we propose a defense method that enhances VLM safety by removing the jailbreak-related shift (JRS-Rem) at inference time. Experiments show that JRS-Rem provides strong defense across multiple scenarios while preserving performance on benign tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/LeeQueue513/JRS-Rem.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Suppression of $^{14}\mathrm{C}$ photon hits in large liquid scintillator detectors via spatiotemporal deep learning
item.description: arXiv:2603.27727v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Liquid scintillator detectors are widely used in neutrino experiments due to their low energy threshold and high energy resolution. Despite the tiny abundance of $^{14}$C in LS, the photons induced by the $\beta$ decay of the $^{14}$C isotope inevitably contaminate the signal, degrading the energy resolution. In this work, we propose three models to tag $^{14}$C photon hits in e$^+$ events with $^{14}$C pile-up, thereby suppressing its impact on the energy resolution at the hit level: a gated spatiotemporal graph neural network and two Transformer-based models with scalar and vector charge encoding. For a simulated test dataset in which each event contains one $^{14}\mathrm{C}$ and one e$^+$ with kinetic energy below 5 MeV, the models achieve $^{14}\mathrm{C}$ recall rates of 25%-48% while maintaining $\mathrm{e}^{+}$ to $^{14}\mathrm{C}$ misidentification below 1%, leading to a large improvement in the resolution of total charge for events where $\mathrm{e}^{+}$ and $^{14}\mathrm{C}$ photon hits strongly overlap in space and time.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: CIDR: A Large-Scale Industrial Source Code Dataset for Software Engineering Research
item.description: arXiv:2605.12153v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present the Curated Industrial Developer Repository (CIDR), a large-scale dataset of real-world software repositories collected from industrial partners. The dataset comprises 4,687 repositories spanning 84 programming languages, totaling 1,033 million raw lines of code (670,3 million logical lines), along with structured metadata at the repository level, full version control history, and engineering-practice attributes such as continuous integration usage and the presence of automated tests. All repositories were collected, filtered, and anonymized through a multi-stage pipeline developed specifically for this purpose. We additionally report an exploratory fine-tuning study that adapts a 3-billion-parameter code language model to CIDR and quantifies the effect on held-out enterprise code. CIDR is intended to support research in code intelligence, software quality analysis, developer tooling, and related software engineering tasks. Access to CIDR is provided under a restricted license; details on eligibility and terms are available at https://fermatix.ai/#Contact.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: RaPD: Resolution-Agnostic Pixel Diffusion via Semantics-Enriched Implicit Representations
item.description: arXiv:2605.15908v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Natural images are continuous, yet most generative models synthesize them on discrete grids, limiting resolution-flexible generation. Continuous neural fields enable resolution-free rendering, but prior methods introduce continuity only at the decoding stage as an interpolation module, leaving the generative latent space discretized and reconstruction-oriented. We propose RaPD (Resolution-agnostic Pixel Diffusion), which performs diffusion in a continuous Neural Image Field (NIF) latent space. RaPD bridges this reconstruction generation gap with Semantic Representation Guidance for generation-aware latent learning and a Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer for coordinate-conditioned, scale-aware rendering. A single denoised latent can be rendered at arbitrary resolutions by changing only the query coordinates, keeping diffusion cost fixed. Experiments demonstrate superior generation quality and resolution scalability.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Advertising to Agents: Measuring Description-Framing Bias in LLM Tool Selection
item.description: arXiv:2605.23916v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI agents often pick tools from registries, where each provider writes its tool's description; we ask whether sales language there changes which tool an agent picks. We built pairs of listings that differ in one way (praise, a verifiable specification, or list order) and asked two OpenAI models to call one tool. In a preregistered study, stacked praise (four kinds) raised a tool's pick rate by about 43 percentage points, matching or beating a verifiable specification. Praise also pulled some picks toward tools whose numeric limit was too small. With identical listings, the first-listed tool was picked about 72 points more often. Structured fields helped agents pick the capable tool; sales text beside them reduced or erased that gain. An exploratory study of five models shows the same direction; a "Sponsored" label dampened it, and a system-prompt warning moved one model. Registries could list limits as fields, hide sales text from agents, and randomize order. Stacked praise replicated on held-out domains; no single kind did after correcting for multiple tests. Preregistered results are provisional until blind phrase ratings are complete, and cover two small models.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Accounting for Purchased Artificial Intelligence Inference in Corporate Greenhouse Gas Inventories: A Token-Based Method
item.description: arXiv:2606.10660v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Purchased artificial intelligence (AI) inference belongs in Scope 3 Category 1 of a corporate greenhouse gas inventory, yet practice omits it or applies a spend-based factor that gives 1.7 to 12.3 times the physical estimate and cannot tell one model or region from another. This paper sets out a token-based method and open dataset: a cradle-to-gate boundary, four tiers of activity data, an effective-token basis, a four-term factor (serving electricity, embodied hardware, data-centre construction, disclosed final training runs) and a rule resolving any model identifier and region to a factor. Inference footprints span twelve times between model classes and nine between regions. The mid-class factor, 0.039 kg of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) per million billed tokens at the world-average grid, is the low end of a stated structural range: a less efficient serving configuration raises it 2.8 times, and replacing the training term with all model development, on its own boundary, gives 1.5 to 2.9 times it. Input bands alone give -18% to +29%. Published per-query energy estimates that can describe a mid-class model are 2.4 to 7.2 times the mid-class energy, above its structural range in four of five rows; those that can describe a frontier-class model bracket it at 0.7 to 1.6 times. Worked examples give 8.5 kg CO2e a year for a 200-person firm, and 2.1 tonnes for fifty developers using agentic coding tools on a mid-class model or 8.3 tonnes on a frontier-class one. The contribution is a traceable figure; accuracy against metered energy is untested.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: AgentRivet: an automated system for producing Rivet routines from journal publications
item.description: arXiv:2606.13535v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Particle physics collider experiments provide Rivet routines as part of the analysis preservation strategy for model-independent measurements. Rivet is a C++ toolkit that allow new theoretical models to be compared to the measurements, thus aiding the development and tuning of Monte Carlo event generators as well as searches for physics beyond the Standard Model. However, analysis coverage is known to be incomplete, with only 39% of measurements having documented and publicly available Rivet routines. In this article, we design and implement an automated workflow based on Large Language Models with the goal of providing the missing routines. This multi-step workflow, referred to as AgentRivet, extracts the physics analysis information from published papers and writes the missing Rivet routines, with intermediate code- and physics- reviews as part of an autonomous quality control. We report the results obtained using commercial Large Language Models, provided by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, for two recent measurements from the ATLAS and CMS experiments. We find that AgentRivet produces competent Rivet routines with few syntax errors. The physics fidelity of the routines is reasonable and follows the explanations given in the relevant publications. Nevertheless, physics-implementation issues do arise and are investigated using the artefacts produced by AgentRivet. The majority of physics implementation issues arise from subtle-but-ambiguous definitions in the given publication, although some models struggle to implement complex observables even when clear definitions are given.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: TORINO: Token Reduction via Interpretable Concept Overlap in Vision-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2607.04593v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across different tasks, but their computational cost is dominated by the large number of visual tokens fed to the language model. Existing token reduction methods rely on attention-based scores or pairwise similarity, without an explicit semantic representation of each token. We introduce TORINO (TOken Reduction via Interpretable coNcept Overlap), a plug-and-play framework for adaptive visual token reduction in VLMs that requires no fine-tuning of the underlying model. TORINO leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to project visual tokens into an interpretable latent space where token relationships can be analyzed through shared concept activations. Specifically, we define concept overlap as the degree of agreement between active SAE latents and use it to group tokens that share semantic content. Reduction within each group is then performed by either pruning or merging, providing a unified framework that preserves semantically important visual information while removing redundancy. Unlike fixed-budget approaches, TORINO dynamically adapts the reduction rate to input complexity, allowing different images to retain different numbers of tokens. Experiments across multiple vision-language benchmarks show that TORINO achieves favorable efficiency-accuracy trade-offs, reducing the number of visual tokens with minimal performance loss. Source code released at https://eidoslab.github.io/TORINO.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Is Your NPU Ready for LLMs? Dissecting the Hidden Efficiency Bottlenecks in Mobile LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2607.05475v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) on mobile devices enhances privacy and reduces latency, but is severely constrained by hardware inefficiencies. We present the first comprehensive, cross-layer measurement study of mobile LLM inference, spanning five mainstream frameworks (e.g., llama.cpp and GENIE) and three hardware backends (CPU, GPU, and NPU). To enable this analysis, we develop PowerBench, a fine-grained profiling tool that measures LLM throughput and provides the first backend-specific energy attribution for mobile LLM inference, going beyond traditional device-level measurements. We further conduct hardware microbenchmarks to characterize the memory-system performance and compute capabilities of mobile CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs. Our study yields three critical insights: (1) Framework-induced performance gaps are substantially amplified on NPUs, reaching up to $10\times$ due to differences in offloading strategies, hardware-underutilizing operators, and activation quantization strategies. (2) We identify a distinct ``phase split,'' in which NPUs excel at compute-bound prefilling, while CPUs outperform all other backends in memory-bound decoding. This split is driven by NPUs' preference for large, fixed-shape workloads, which conflicts with the small-kernel, dynamic nature of decoding. (3) Backend-specific profiling uncovers substantial scheduling headroom missed by prior work. Suboptimal thread configurations, uncoordinated NPU sleep latencies, and CPU polling intervals result in unnecessary energy consumption. For example, tuning CPU frequency alone reduces energy consumption by up to $39.7\%$. Leveraging these findings, we estimate that an energy-oriented configuration can reduce energy consumption by up to $53.2\%$ on the NPU backend across three datasets, highlighting the substantial potential for further efficiency improvements in mobile LLM deployment.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Do Multi-Agent LLMs Explore Each Other?
item.description: arXiv:2607.11250v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Exploration is essential for reliable autonomy in multi-agent systems, yet it remains unclear whether large language model (LLM) agents can explore effectively when interacting with one another. We show that modern LLM agents often fail to do so, exhibiting myopic and polarized interaction patterns that lead to suboptimal coordination and increased regret. We formalize this challenge as the Multi-Agent Exploration problem, modeling it as a partially observable stochastic game (POSG), in which agents must probe peers to infer their capabilities and identify effective interaction strategies. To address this, we introduce Multi-Agent Contextual Exploration (MACE), a lightweight framework that explicitly promotes exploration through structured peer selection. Across both contextual and parametric diversity settings, exploration behavior and downstream task performance substantially improve when MACE is applied. We further provide theoretical insight that MACE achieves a sublinear expected-regret bound. Overall, our results highlight a fundamental limitation of current LLM agents and underscore the importance of explicitly guided exploration for reliable multi-agent autonomy.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: KAYROS: An Anytime and Exact Open-Source Solver for Duration-Minimization Time-Dependent Vehicle Routing. A Technical Report and a Case Study in Human-AI Engineering
item.description: arXiv:2607.23116v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Time-dependent routing recognizes that the same journey can take a different time depending on when it begins. Under duration minimization, even the departure time of each vehicle becomes a decision. Exact methods for this setting exist in the literature, but researchers and practitioners have lacked a ready-to-use open solver that combines rich piecewise-linear travel times, early feasible solutions and optimality claims. KAYROS fills this gap with two modes on one checker-consistent engine: an Iterated Local Search that streams improving solutions and a Branch-Price-and-Cut method that can issue computational optimality certificates under explicit arithmetic and search assumptions. It installs with one command and has no proprietary dependency. The public MAMUT-routing store currently contains 704 KAYROS certificates under a four-solve publication protocol, which has also led to the retraction and repair of invalid earlier claims. The report presents two complementary benchmark contributions to MAMUT-routing. The first integrates Blauth2024, a benchmark from the literature whose travel times derive from measured Uber speeds, for which KAYROS provides new best-known solutions on all 40 instances. The second proposes Poryos2026, a new benchmark of 1,080 paired static and time-dependent instances built from OpenStreetMap road networks and controlled synthetic traffic. Finally, the report describes the intensive human-AI collaboration behind this work and the verification practices that kept its outputs independently verifiable.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Efficient LLM-Generated Shuttling Compilers for Complex Trapped-Ion Architectures
item.description: arXiv:2607.24714v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Trapped-ion quantum computers rely on shuttling compilers, which cast an input algorithm into a sequence of ion-qubit movements within a given architecture. We present the first study in which a single frontier large language model (LLM), Claude Opus 4.7, generates and iteratively refines the Python code of shuttling compilers from written specifications. Starting with a compiler for (i) a linear segmented trap, we extend it to (ii) a trap with junctions, and finally achieve efficient compilation for (iii) a broad class of connected trap graphs. The compilers for the more general cases are seeded with code from the previous ones. We benchmark the LLM-generated compilers against state-of-the-art hand-crafted ones using a common suite of quantum circuits. The number of shuttling timesteps is reduced by up to 72% for (i) and up to 43% for (ii). For the broad case (iii) of freely connected architectures, we find large variations in the required number of shuttling timesteps, depending on the connectivity. A densely connected, junction-rich architecture yields up to an order-of-magnitude reduction in shuttling timesteps compared to a corridor-like one. Repeating the complete generation and evaluation with a second frontier LLM, Claude Fable 5, reproduces these findings, with the Fable 5 compilers surpassing the hand-crafted ones more often on the largest circuits. Our results show that an unmodified frontier LLM can produce working, correct, and competitive shuttling compilers without additional manual algorithmic engineering. Generating compilers this way reduces the development time for new architectures from several months to a few days.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Demystifying When and Why VLAs Fail in Contact-Rich Tasks and How to Fix Them
item.description: arXiv:2608.01402v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We address the problem of understanding when and why Vision-Language-Action models struggle with contact-rich manipulation tasks that require precise physical interaction. Prior work has primarily focused on addressing contact failures through force-augmented architectures and training-time regularizers, yet the factors contributing to these failures remain underexplored. We identify two distinct failure modes underlying this gap. Precision failures occur when policies struggle to produce the small, accurate corrective actions required during contact and force failures occur when policies fail to respond to contact forces. To address these failures, we propose FACT. During post-training, FACT increases low noise sampling to improve fine action prediction and incorporates structured force conditioning to guide action generation using contact state and force history. FACT achieves an average success rate of 66% across five contact-rich tasks against 41% for the best prior baseline, in an evaluation spanning almost 2,500 real-world rollouts.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: MANGO-Grasp: Mahalanobis Fields over Geometry-Oriented 3D Gaussians for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasping
item.description: arXiv:2608.02014v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cross-embodiment dexterous grasping aims to synthesize stable grasps across heterogeneous multi-fingered hands with little or no embodiment-specific tuning. Existing interaction-centric methods achieve promising results, but their object representations often underrepresent local surface geometry, hand descriptors do not explicitly capture both morphology and kinematics, and hand-object interaction modeling is typically isotropic. We propose MANGO-Grasp, an anisotropic interaction framework that represents objects as geometry-oriented 3D Gaussian primitives to better preserve local surface geometry, and encodes hands into pretrained descriptors that capture both morphology and kinematics. Hand-object interaction is modeled using anisotropic Mahalanobis fields that reflect the directional nature of contact and guide a shared optimization for grasp realization across embodiments. On the CMAP and MultiGripperGrasp benchmarks, MANGO-Grasp outperforms the strongest seen-hand baseline by up to 8.24 percentage points in simulation. It also transfers zero-shot to the unseen SharpaWave hand, improving over the strongest zero-shot baseline by up to 16.57 percentage points, and achieves 86% success in real-world experiments. The code and additional materials will be made available upon publication at https://connor-zh.github.io/MANGO-Grasp/.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Rescene: stable century-long climate emulation from a frozen weather model
item.description: arXiv:2608.09971v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine-learning weather models now match or exceed operational numerical prediction in the medium range, but when they are run freely for years they drift, blow up or lose their variability, and dedicated climate emulators are expensive to train. Here we present Rescene, a 0.4 M-parameter wrapper that turns a frozen 1.5$^\circ$, 6-hourly, 69-variable weather model into a stochastic climate emulator. A deterministic slow clock anchors the frozen model to a calendar climatology, and a band-limited AR(1) perturbation, whose spectral envelope is fixed to the observed anomaly spectrum, restores the weather that anchoring removes. A 100-year, 8-member Rescene run shows no detectable drift ($-0.004 \pm 0.014$ K per 100 years), and on the 2022 test year the 16-member ensemble is calibrated (spread/skill 0.89, 0.97 and 0.93 for Z500, T2m and MSLP) with an extratropical synoptic amplitude of 97% of ERA5 on the tuning year. The free run reproduces the geography of day-to-day variability (pattern correlation 0.83 for Z500) and 71% of the observed blocking frequency, where the deterministic wrapper alone has none. Interventions on the frozen operator show a scale-local, approximately linear response in which Z500 perturbations grow upscale 6--14 times more than downscale per 6 h. All constants are fitted on a training year against a rule declared beforehand, and we show that common evaluation shortcuts would have overstated variability and skill. Rescene makes an existing weather model usable for century-long ensembles at negligible training cost.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: ADEPT: Accelerating Dexterity via Pre-Training and Post-Training using Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2608.19182v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce Accelerating Dexterity via Pre-Training (ADEPT), a large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) framework for learning sim-to-real transferable dexterity across high degree-of-freedom (DoF) robot embodiments that can solve long-horizon tasks directly from raw visuo-tactile perception. ADEPT pretrains a dexterous policy on a generic object reposing task, then post-trains downstream policies with this pretrained behavior as a prior. ADEPT enables learning new behaviors that are otherwise difficult to discover from scratch on multi-fingered robots and avoids learning the same set of skills over again for every new downstream task. The pretrained policy zero-shots the reposing phase of downstream tasks, but na\"ive RL fine-tuning rapidly degrades this capability during transfer. We address this with a stable post-training recipe combining behavior-cloning distillation, critic warm-up, and conservative on-policy updates. To safely exploit the full kinematic dexterity, we introduce a joint-space Geometric Fabric that mediates between the RL policy and the robot. We distill post-trained teachers into perceptive students that zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on two embodiments: a 23 DoF Kuka-Allegro with two RGB cameras, and a 29 DoF Flexiv-Sharpa with two RGB cameras and five vision-based tactile sensors, and can solve long-horizon tasks from challenging initial states with dexterity at human-level speed.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Mind the Phase: Effective Rank and Representation Health in Legged Locomotion
item.description: arXiv:2609.06958v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning has become the leading paradigm in legged locomotion, enabling complex behaviors from backflips to parkour via massively parallel simulation. Under PPO's non-stationarity, shallow networks remain the de facto architecture, supported by carefully staged environments; nevertheless, the representations learned by these policies remain poorly understood, specifically the relation to motion produced on hardware. In this work, we empirically study locomotion policies through the effective rank of the network Jacobian and show that conditioning rank on gait phase exposes representation structures invisible from a global rank. In particular, we find that architectural choices, namely observation and layer normalization with residual connections, allocate more than one additional dimension of effective rank to swing-dominant states than to stance-dominant states, which is mostly absent in vanilla MLPs. Building on this, we propose practical recommendations to convert these into diagnostics for healthier and smoother policies. In practice, this results in lower joint jitter, up to $2$x, not only in simulation, but also on a physical Spot. More broadly, our findings show that how a policy distributes its capacity across the gait cycle is closely tied to its health and sim-to-real transfer.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: How Children Design and Reason about Trustworthy AI Chatbots
item.description: arXiv:2609.25244v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Children increasingly interact with AI chatbots, making trust calibration essential to AI literacy. Prior research has examined children's trust in AI mainly as users evaluating systems built by others, rather than as designers of their own chatbots. We developed a chatbot-building environment with adjustable trust-relevant traits (e.g., confidence, transparency, formality, assertiveness), rules, and persona. We conducted mixed-methods study with 115 learners (ages 8-18) who made 119 chatbots. We examined how children configured their chatbots, reasoned about trustworthiness, and how closely chatbot behavior aligned with their designs. Younger students (age 10-13) set significantly higher confidence than older students (age 14-18), and some deliberately built chatbots that gave wrong answers on purpose, yet still called them trustworthy, arguing that a chatbot does what it was built to do. Younger students equated trust with purpose-fulfillment, while older students linked it to transparent, calibrated design. Students also calibrated academic chatbots to be more transparent and formal than hobby chatbots. We identify seven design dimensions describing what children believe makes a chatbot trustworthy, and discuss implications for AI literacy tools.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: NutriVision: Ingredient-Conditioned Fusion and Prediction for Single-Image Food Nutrition Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2609.33076v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Nutrition estimation is a fundamental task in consumer diet tracking, clinical dietetics, chronic disease management, sports and hospital nutrition, and broader food computing systems. The existing approaches have progressed along two largely separate axes, vision models that rely on calibrated RGB-depth captures and ingredient-aware methods that use textual cues but use limited multimodal fusion. We introduce NutriVision, an end-to-end framework that leverages visual geometry and ingredient semantics to estimate calories, mass, fat content, carbohydrates, and protein from a single RGB image and an optional ingredient list. It obtains the unavailable depth modality using DepthAnything-V3 and encodes ingredient descriptions using CLIP. It integrates three complementary mechanisms: (1) an \emph{Ingredient-Conditioned Frequency-Aligned Fusion Module (IC-FAFM)}, which uses textual guidance to reweight and align RGB-depth frequency components; (2) an \emph{Ingredient-Aware Mask-based Prediction Head (IA-MPH)}, whose gating and channel masks are conditioned on food identity; and (3) modality-specific \emph{Internal Semantic Modeling (ISM)} blocks. On the Nutrition5k dataset, NutriVision achieves a mean PMAE of $\mathbf{13.60\pm0.10\%}$, outperforming our IGSMNet implementation by $0.89$ percentage points and OmniFood8k by $2.90$ percentage points (both $p<0.001$). The module-level ablations identify the ingredient-aware prediction head as the primary architectural contributor, improving mean PMAE by $1.50\pm0.17$ percentage points ($p<0.001$). These results demonstrate that ingredient-conditioned prediction and frequency-aware RGB-depth fusion provide measurable gains for single-image nutrient estimation. More broadly, NutriVision offers a practical route toward nutrition-assessment systems that exploit geometric and semantic cues without requiring specialized depth-sensing hardware
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: CollabFlow: Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Collaboration
item.description: arXiv:2609.38662v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) lets a system improve from its own outcomes; in LLM-based multi-agent systems, Agents refine one another within a task, and outcomes improve how they collaborate across tasks. However, existing multi-agent collaboration leaves this loop open: collaboration is pre-defined at the operator level, topology-only learning keeps verbatim exchange that propagates errors, and reward maximization on a system's own outcomes concentrates on a few teams. To address these challenges, we propose CollabFlow, an RSI system of Learned Agent Collaboration: a trainable Collab-Director constructs teams of complete Agents, a frozen executor runs them, and each round's outcomes retrain the director. Within each round, the edges of a collaboration graph carry protocols of Evidence-Conditioned Communication: a receiver adopts a differing answer only when the sender's evidence is stronger by a margin, so the director learns who communicates and how. Across rounds, we further propose Collaborative Trajectory Balance (CTB), a flow-based objective that credits each team once across its construction orders and targets a reward-proportional distribution over teams, so several good teams stay in play. We also bound how far this self-generated target moves between rounds, which shrinks as records accumulate. On twelve datasets, CollabFlow outperforms all baselines and keeps improving across rounds. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CollabFlow-631E.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: RoboHarness: A Simple Harness Outperforms VLA and World Action Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.14018v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has opened a path toward generalist embodied AI, raising the question of how LLMs can act in the physical world. One straightforward approach is training the model to generate actions: collect robot-action data and video demonstration, refine LLM architecture with an action head, and train a vision-language-action (VLA) model at scale. However, we argue that coding agents have the potential to realize generalist embodied manipulation. All they need is a simple yet effective robot harness. We present RoboHarness: a robotic harness that gives LLM agents a visual-geometric control panel so that they can directly understand and invoke embodied tasks. With RoboHarness, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next outperforms state-of-the-art VLA models on BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 tasks. The implementation is open source.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: VideoHarness-SRSI: Structured Recursive Self-Improvement for Video Understanding Harness
item.description: arXiv:2610.19424v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We first introduce VHarness-BRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves video harnesses around a frozen vision-language model. Analyzing over 4,000 evolved candidates, we find it competitive with hand-engineered systems but identify three interconnected failure modes: validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap. We trace all three to a common root: the same imperfect validation evidence drives both harness revisions and the proposer's search strategy. We therefore propose VHarness-SRSI, an evidence-governed framework in which every search decision rests on evidence that is transferable, sufficient, and gathered before the search commits. It restricts the proposer to content-free feedback, informs exploration with instrumented warm-up experiments, and develops mechanisms in isolated probe-race branches before factorial composition and joint refinement. Across four video understanding benchmarks, VideoHarness-SRSI improves the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to VideoHarness-BRSI and reduces the mean validation-test gap by 37.9%. Reliable harness evolution thus depends on how search is organized and informed, not only on how well it optimizes validation performance.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Causal Integrated Gradients: Scalable Feature Attribution Along Causal Paths
item.description: arXiv:2610.22126v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing feature attribution methods that account for feature dependencies do not scale to high dimensions. We propose causal integrated gradients (CIG) and causal expected gradients (CEG), which extend integrated gradients to incorporate prior causal structure among input features while retaining its computational efficiency and, under conditions on the causal graph, its axiomatic guarantees. In many settings, some causal structure between features is already known, for example, that a transcription factor causally regulates a target gene's expression. Yet existing gradient-based methods cannot exploit this structure, instead crediting a feature's downstream effects over its true upstream cause, such as ranking the target gene above the transcription factor that regulates it. Our key idea is to embed this causal structure by routing the integration path along the causal graph. The method thereby decomposes each feature's attribution into a direct effect and effects mediated through its causal descendants. We evaluate CIG in three settings of increasing realism. First, on a synthetic benchmark with a known causal model, CIG's attributions best match the ground-truth causal effect from Pearl's do-calculus, matching the accuracy of causal Shapley values at a fraction of the computational cost. Second, on simulated single-cell gene expression data with a known gene regulatory network (Dyngen), CIG most accurately recovers the transcription factors driving the simulation. Third, on real interferon-$\beta$ stimulation data, where only an approximate causal graph is available, CIG better prioritizes the transcription factors driving the measured response than DeepSHAP and integrated gradients. Together, these results show that incorporating causal structure into gradient-based attributions recovers upstream drivers that existing methods miss, without sacrificing scalability.

item.title: CausalEvo: Causal Skill Self-Evolution for Health LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.21016v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for health can accumulate reusable textual skills from task feedback, such as calculation criteria, measurement time points, and formula units. Deciding which skills to retain is consequential: useful rules improve later answers, while faulty generalizations propagate errors. We propose CausalEvo, a method for causal skill self-evolution that estimates the relative effects of deliberately changed skill sets while holding the model weights, feedback cases, and rule count fixed. At each evolution step, a frozen LLM proposes candidate rules, which are pooled with the incumbent skills so that the current skill set remains a feasible choice. Paired skill replacements against shared background rules are scored on the same feedback cases; least squares converts the score differences into relative skill values, and the top-ranked rules are retained, favoring incumbents on ties. A decision-loss bound separates candidate support, approximation, and estimation errors. On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks with 120 held-out cases, CausalEvo achieves 60.00% accuracy, compared with 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills. Across the recorded training configurations, which use different optimization budgets, it consumes 55.6% fewer training tokens than SkillOpt. Gains concentrate in particular calculations alongside regressions on others, and paired accuracy intervals include zero. CausalEvo turns task feedback into controlled decisions about skill retention and replacement. Project repository: https://github.com/txbrook/CausalEvo
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Digital Twin-Conditioned RSS-Fingerprint Localization in Cell-Free Millimeter-Wave Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.20933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital twins (DTs) can generate dense synthetic fingerprints for localization via ray tracing, yet the sim-to-real domain gap limits their direct use, particularly in cell-free millimeter-wave (mmWave) deployments where distributed geometries and blockage-induced sparsity widen the mismatch. We propose DT-conditioned (DTCond), a framework that fuses real and DT beam-domain fingerprints as complementary inputs through per-domain encoders, learnable per-access point (AP) attention, and calibrated uncertainty. We derive oracle and pipeline Cram\'er-Rao bounds (CRBs) for DT-aided fingerprint localization, proving that DT information strictly tightens the positioning bound whenever spatial structure is preserved, with a heteroscedastic refinement that tightens the bound by a further 9.1%. On a real 28 GHz cell-free testbed, the deployable two-stage pipeline, which reads the DT fingerprint at a coarse k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) estimate, achieves 0.284 m mean error against 0.313 m for real-only k-NN. With the DT fingerprint read at the true position (oracle input), DT conditioning achieves 0.186 m mean error, validated through a ten-method ablation against domain-adaptation (DA) and transfer-learning baselines, and a 48% improvement on unseen regions. Multi-user self-attention provides 31-41% per-user gain for emulated simultaneous users, and progressive calibration reduces the measurement budget by 50%. As a use case, localization drives network configuration in closed loop. Between beam sweeps, a DT updated from measured RSS and read at the tracked position estimate selects the 3 of 81 beam pairs that each AP trains. With 49 calibration anchors in the update, the mean beam-selection loss stays below 1 dB over 2 m of motion, whereas reusing the last sweep loses 2.7 dB after 1 m.

item.title: Orientation-Aware Deep Learning Framework for RSSI-Based Indoor Localization in RIS-Aided mmWave Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.21043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-aided millimeter wave (mmWave) systems provide directional measurements of received power for indoor localization, but device orientation changes the fingerprints. This work proposes an orientation-aware dual-stream gated (O-DSG) deep learning framework for received signal strength indicator (RSSI)-based indoor localization. An orientation classifier estimates device orientation from RSSI, so inference needs only received power. An embedding of the predicted angle and posterior entropy controls feature modulation and soft expert gating. Parallel convolutional and statistical streams are fused through bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) processing and temporal attention. Single-user measurements in an indoor laboratory at 28 GHz under non-line-of-sight (NLoS) conditions yield a median localization error of 0.141 m, a 25.8% improvement over the closest evaluated baseline (supplied with the measured orientation), and 92.3% orientation classification accuracy across four discrete classes. In spatial regions withheld from training, O-DSG has an average median error of 0.247 m, against 0.392 m for a validation-selected sequence model. A separate offline evaluation constructs non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-style power mixtures from the single-user measurements and measures localization accuracy and computational scaling with up to eight emulated users whose power contributions overlap, under the specified mixture model.

item.title: PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.21390v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed at the edge to support complex tasks that require collaboration and information exchange among multiple agents. However, when task contexts are passed across agents, shared context that has already been processed by upstream agents often needs to be prefilled again, resulting in substantial redundant computation. Reusing an already prefilled key--value (KV) cache can avoid this recomputation, but requires the reusable KV state to be transferred across the network before the receiving agent can begin generation. Under strict time-to-first-token (TTFT) deadlines and unreliable edge links, delivering the complete KV cache may be infeasible, making it necessary to prioritize and protect the most valuable KV information within a limited transmission budget. This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that jointly exploits model-side KV importance and transport-side reliability. PriorityFEC first constructs a utility-aware source stream by placing high-utility KV blocks at earlier transmission positions. It then protects the ordered stream using a feedback-adaptive Streaming Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) mechanism, which schedules repair packets according to receiver feedback before the TTFT deadline. We implement PriorityFEC on a distributed edge LLM serving prototype and evaluate it with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple datasets. Results show that PriorityFEC achieves superior task quality over the compared transport schemes, with its advantages becoming particularly pronounced under stringent deadline constraints. These results demonstrate the importance of jointly optimizing KV-cache utility and deadline-aware transport reliability when reusable LLM state must be handed off across unreliable edge networks.

item.title: Decoding What iOS Location Services Send to Apple: An LLM Is an Unreliable Analyst but a Useful Toolmaker
item.description: arXiv:2610.21597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reverse engineering the data formats used by mobile software is skilled and slow, and using AI to assist with it is attractive. We evaluate this for the protobuf messages that an iPhone sends to Apple's location services. Working from Apple's binaries, we use two frontier models (Claude Opus 4.8, Codex GPT Sol 5.6) to reconstruct the schemas of protobufs observed in network traffic. The great majority of the schemas contain substantial errors, and these are hard to detect because the schemas are internally consistent. Direct AI use is therefore unsuitable for forensic and privacy analysis. AI can, however, write reliable analysis tools when their output can be validated. We use Claude to write a Python tool, Extractor, that reliably recovers protobuf schemas from Apple binaries. We validate it against binaries compiled from schemas with known answers, previously published schemas, and network measurements. We demonstrate the use of Extractor to decode and analyse the location services network traffic of a jailbroken iPhone 8 (iOS 16.7.11).

item.title: Coverage-Preserving Self-Healing in Partially Observable 3D UAV Swarm Networks via an Advection-Diffusion Graph Transformer
item.description: arXiv:2610.22085v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the resilience and self-healing of unmanned aerial vehicle swarm communication networks under severe network partitioning in complex and adversarial environments. To address limited global observability after damage, we develop a damage-state inference mechanism that enables the ground control station (GCS) to infer global failures from sparse local reports without transmitting location-sensitive coordinates. To recover multi-cluster partitioned topologies, we then propose AdDiff-GT, a physics-inspired graph Transformer that incorporates advection-diffusion dynamics into a node-supernode hybrid graph. Local message propagation captures intra-cluster structural relationships, while global attention models inter-cluster interactions. A weighted composite loss jointly considers connectivity restoration, maneuvering cost, motion consistency, inter-cluster coordination, and spatial preservation during model training. We further develop a meta-learning strategy for transferable initialization across damage patterns and swarm scales, enabling efficient online GCS adaptation and distributed airborne inference. Simulations on 8,000 partitioned scenarios, including 5,000 large-scale cases, show that AdDiff-GT achieves effective topology recovery and spatial preservation over six representative baselines. Meta-learning reduces online planning overhead with a minor increase in recovery steps, balancing prior knowledge transfer and online adaptation.

item.title: Online Tree Caching
item.description: arXiv:1602.08563v3 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We initiate the study of a natural and practically relevant new variant of online caching where the to-be-cached items can have dependencies. We assume that the universe is a tree $T$ and items are tree nodes; we require that if a node $v$ is cached then the whole subtree $T(v)$ rooted at $v$ is cached as well. This theoretical problem finds an immediate application in the context of forwarding table optimization in IP routing and software-defined networks. We present an elegant online deterministic algorithm TC for this problem, and rigorously prove that its competitive ratio is $O(\mathrm{height}(T) \cdot k_{\mathrm{ONL}}/(k_{\mathrm{ONL}}-k_{\mathrm{OPT}}+1))$, where $k_{\mathrm{ONL}}$ and $k_{\mathrm{OPT}}$ denote the cache sizes of an online and the optimal offline algorithm, respectively. The result is optimal up to a factor of $O(\mathrm{height}(T))$. We complement the theoretical analysis with an empirical study on synthetic workloads and CAIDA backbone traffic, illustrating the trade-off between hit rate and cache-update cost.

item.title: MAppPrint: Robust and Real-time Mobile App Fingerprinting via Traffic Behavior Correlation Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.22148v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mobile apps have become ubiquitous in daily life. Despite communication encryption, app fingerprinting (AF) attacks can still enable adversaries to infer the apps in use by analyzing patterns of encrypted network traffic. However, existing AF attacks suffer from three critical limitations that hinder their practical effectiveness: (i) the inability to capture app-specific traffic dependencies, rendering traffic fingerprints fragile under dynamic networking conditions; (ii) the neglect of latency and throughput considerations, resulting in inefficient real-time user tracking; and (iii) the incapacity to handle mixed traffic generated by multi-app concurrency. In this paper, we propose MAppPrint, a robust and real-time app fingerprinting framework. MAppPrint introduces a behavior-level traffic fingerprint, i.e., Traffic Behavior Correlation Graph (TBCG), which models app traffic by capturing unit traffic behaviors and their correlations, thereby providing reliable app fingerprints. To enable real-time fingerprinting, MAppPrint incorporates a fingerprint compression algorithm that transforms each TBCG into a compact graph by selectively aggregating redundant information. Furthermore, MAppPrint employs an unsupervised decomposition strategy to disentangle mixed traffic generated by multi-app concurrency, enabling unified identification of both single-app and multi-app traffic. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that MAppPrint achieves 4.9~13.9% improvement in AF precision and 3~6 times improvement in timeliness over state-of-the-art methods. Meanwhile, MAppPrint is robust in dynamic networking conditions, while achieving a throughput of 10.5 GB/s and a prediction latency of 0.68 seconds.

item.title: Minimizing Age of Incorrect Information in Pull-Based Remote Estimation of a Markov Source
item.description: arXiv:2610.22265v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we consider a discrete-time pull-based remote estimation system involving an information source and a remote monitor where the information source is a finite-state irreducible discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC) process. In this system, the remote monitor sends a pull request towards the source which responds by sampling its process so as to transmit the sampled values towards the monitor through a delay channel, encapsulated in information packets. We consider i) zero delay (ZD) and ii) unit delay (UD) channels, where the packet transmission times are zero and one slot, respectively. For remote estimation, we use the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator, and for quantifying its performance, we use the mean age of incorrect information (MAoII) which is a recently proposed freshness and mismatch metric that penalizes an incorrect estimation along with its duration. Our goal is to obtain pull policies so as to minimize MAoII under a long-run sampling rate constraint. For the ZD model, we propose a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) formulation of the problem, which allows us to find the optimum observation-dependent pull policy. On the other hand, the UD channel prevents the monitor from possessing perfect information on the actual AoII process at any given time, and the SMDP formulation of the ZD channel cannot readily be used for the UD model. For the system with the UD channel, we first provide a numerical algorithm to calculate the MAoII and the average sampling rate for a given observation-dependent pull policy. For the optimization of the underlying remote estimation system, we use the joint distribution of the age and source processes to be obtained from the history of all observations, termed as belief. Subsequently, we propose a belief-dependent policy obtained via the belief-MDP formulation and a constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) algorithm.

item.title: How Feasible are Passive Network Attacks on 5G Networks and Beyond? A Survey
item.description: arXiv:2512.20622v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Privacy concerns around 5G, the latest generation of mobile networks, are growing, with fears that its deployment may increase exposure to privacy risks. This perception is largely driven by the use of denser deployments of small antenna systems, which enable highly accurate data collection at higher speeds and closer proximity to mobile users. At the same time, 5G's unique radio communication features can make the reproduction of known network attacks more challenging. In particular, passive network attacks, which do not involve direct interaction with the target network and are therefore nearly impossible to detect, remain a pressing concern. Such attacks can reveal sensitive information about users, their devices, and active applications, which may then be exploited through known vulnerabilities or spear-phishing schemes. This survey examines the feasibility of passive network attacks in 5G and beyond (B5G/6G) networks, with emphasis on two major categories: information extraction (system identification, website and application fingerprinting) and geolocation (user identification and position tracking). These attacks are well documented and reproducible in existing wireless and mobile systems, including short-range networks (IEEE 802.11) and, to a lesser extent, LTE. Current evidence suggests that while such attacks remain theoretically possible in 5G, their practical execution is significantly constrained by directional beamforming, high-frequency propagation characteristics, and encryption mechanisms. For B5G and early 6G networks, the lack of public tools and high hardware cost currently renders these attacks infeasible in practice, which highlights a critical gap in our understanding of future network threat models.

item.title: Clock-Free Stochastic Scheduling for Real-Time Synchronized Content Delivery
item.description: arXiv:2610.15114v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Real-time synchronized content delivery is critical for applications such as cloud gaming, collaborative mixed reality, and live streaming, where a server must ensure that a group of users perceives the same content simultaneously for each delivery. Due to heterogeneous and unpredictable network delays, ensuring synchronization is highly challenging. We propose a clock-free scheduling framework that introduces latency compensation to control the server's delivery time for each user, aiming to maximize synchronization performance (i.e., minimizing the gap between the maximum and minimum latencies) while maintaining a low overall latency cost. Unlike prior work requiring synchronized clocks or client-side timestamps, our approach uses only acknowledgment feedback, enabling flexible deployment across diverse environments. We formulate the problem as a convex stochastic optimization with a non-smooth objective. To solve the problem, we employ the stochastic proximal point (SPP) algorithm that updates the delay compensation, using only the previous latency samples, rather than the latency distribution. By exploiting the subproblem structure, we apply ADMM to enable efficient updates with per-iteration complexity of at most $\mathcal{O}(N\log N)$, where $N$ is the number of users. We establish a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K})$, where $K$ is the number of content deliveries for transmission. The framework is further extended to handle transmission failures, where packet loss results in successful delivery to only a subset of users. Finally, simulations using both synthetic and real-world latency traces demonstrate the consistent superiority of our algorithm against baseline methods.

item.title: Multimodal Remote Inference
item.description: arXiv:2508.07555v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider a remote inference system with multiple modalities, where a multimodal machine learning (ML) model performs real-time inference using features collected from remote sensors. When sensor observations evolve dynamically over time, fresh features are critical for inference tasks. However, timely delivery of features from all modalities is often infeasible under limited network resources. To address this challenge, we formulate a multimodal scheduling problem to minimize the ML model's inference error. We model this error as a general function of the Age of Information (AoI) vector, where AoI quantifies data freshness. We cast the problem as a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) and derive an equivalent reformulation with a reduced state set. We then show that the problem has fundamentally different chain structures in the two-modality and multi-modality cases. For the two-modality case, we prove that the optimal policy has an index-based threshold structure. For the general multi-modality case (two or more modalities), we develop an optimal switching-type policy (OPT-ST), which is computed using a multichain policy iteration algorithm (MPI). To further reduce complexity, we also develop two low-complexity policies: the round-robin-like switching-type policy (RR-ST) and the round-robin-like threshold policy (RR-Thres). Numerical results show that OPT-ST achieves the lowest inference error among all baselines, with reductions of up to 80.3%. In a five-modality case, RR-ST and RR-Thres achieve $5.2\times$ and $89.8\times$ speedups in offline computation over OPT-ST, respectively, at the cost of increasing the inference error by 23.3% and 38.6%, respectively.

item.title: Declared but Unaccountable: Measuring the Seller-Identity Gap in Advertising Supply-Chain Transparency
item.description: arXiv:2610.14661v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Public advertising transparency relies on a minimum accountability condition: an account authorized by a publisher in ads$.$txt or app-ads$.$txt should appear in the applicable sellers$.$json registry. When an available registry omits the declared seller ID, the authorization remains visible and machine-readable, but its public verification path breaks. We call this failure the seller-identity gap. We measure the gap using 233.4 million normalized advertising-transparency records and an absent-only, coverage-aware evidence rule. A declaration enters the numerator only when the applicable registry is available and omits its seller ID; unavailable, malformed, confidential, and other non-evaluable states remain separate. The resulting row-level floor is 24.25% in a high-popularity, low-removal reference population and 30.71% among publishers associated with at least 100 copyright-removal requests, a 6.45 percentage-point increase. The gap then remains near one third at stricter cumulative thresholds. Standardizing the populations to common weights over 1,469 shared ad systems reduces the primary contrast to 4.65 points: about 72% remains within systems, while 28% forms a composition-associated residual. We connect these population estimates to recurring seller-account coordinates, byte-identical declaration configurations, and provenance-bearing case packets. We frame this declaration-centered investigative use of public advertising records as Ad Transparency Intelligence: it reconstructs declared supply-chain relationships, identifies where public verification stops, and prioritizes evidence for corroboration without equating correlation with attribution. Advertising transparency supports accountability and investigation only when visible authorizations remain publicly verifiable.

item.title: Forensic Analysis of the HackRF One with PortaPack Mayhem Firmware
item.description: arXiv:2610.20647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software-defined radios (SDRs) have become an inexpensive, portable platform for replay attacks, location spoofing and jamming. The HackRF One can operate stand-alone when fitted with a PortaPack interface board running the open-source Mayhem firmware. No peer-reviewed study has addressed the forensic analysis of this device family. This work establishes, at source-code level, where forensically relevant data reside on the microSD card of a device running Mayhem v2.0.1, in which format, when they are written and how they should be interpreted. The methodology is applied to an SD card image that the author acquired from their own device after four months of real use, and every inference is drawn from the image alone. The workflow covers timestamp rules that depend on the real-time clock (RTC) battery state, traces of on-device trimming and text editing, cluster-level recovery of deleted in-phase/quadrature (IQ) captures, and decoding of recorded signals cross-checked with an independent decoder. In the example image, the final part of a deleted IQ capture and a trimmed-away capture segment are recovered, and six captures are attributed to a single rolling-code on-off keying (OOK) transmitter sharing one 32-bit identifier. The study provides practitioners with an artifact catalogue, interpretation rules and acquisition recommendations.

item.title: Empirical Evaluation of Machine Learning for Cloud Cryptojacking Detection: Effects of Preprocessing and Evaluation Protocols
item.description: arXiv:2610.20658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied to cloud cryptojacking detection. Classical machine learning models remain among the most widely used approaches for cloud cryptojacking detection. This paper presents an empirical evaluation of six widely used classical machine learning models for AI-based cloud cryptojacking detection under different preprocessing and evaluation settings. Because no public cloud-native cryptojacking dataset is currently available, experiments were conducted using two publicly available proxy datasets, DS2OS and NSL-KDD. The evaluated models include Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, Decision Tree, and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN). Experimental results show that preprocessing choices and evaluation protocols have a measurable impact on model performance. On DS2OS, removing identifier-related features reduced the accuracy of most models to approximately 96%, while KNN achieved higher accuracy with lower attack recall. On NSL-KDD, models obtained 77 to 80\% accuracy on the official test set containing unseen attack types, compared with above 99.5% under a random train-test split. Attack-class precision, recall, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) further provide complementary insights into classifier performance beyond overall accuracy. The results provide an empirical comparison of commonly used classical machine learning models under consistent experimental settings and offer insights into how preprocessing, dataset selection, and evaluation methodology influence reported performance.

item.title: Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network for Interpretable Big Data Analytics and Secure Cloud Decision-Making Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.20661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Big data analytics supports modern intelligent systems, but model complexity and limited transparency can undermine interpretability, trust, and security in decision-making. This paper presents the Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network, a deep learning framework that integrates temporal, relational, and contextual features with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) mechanisms. The architecture combines one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) for temporal feature extraction, Transformer encoders for contextual modeling, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for inter-feature dependency analysis. An attention-based fusion mechanism integrates these representations. Class Activation Mapping (CAM) and an explanation loss are incorporated to improve interpretability and explanation consistency. The framework is designed for deployment in a federated cloud architecture, using homomorphic encryption and blockchain-based auditing to support data privacy and accountability. Experimental evaluations across healthcare, finance, and energy datasets report 98.42% accuracy, 97.9% precision, 98.1% recall, and a 98.0% F1-score, outperforming the evaluated CNN-LSTM, Transformer-only, and XGBoost baselines. Under projected gradient descent (PGD) adversarial perturbations, the model reportedly retains accuracy above 91.5%. Scalability experiments report throughput of 80,000 messages per second with latency below 200 milliseconds. These results suggest that the proposed framework has potential for interpretable and secure cloud-based decision-support systems.

item.title: CascadeLedger: Counterfactual Auditing of Information and Resource Integrity in LLM Cascades
item.description: arXiv:2610.20668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce CascadeLedger, a counterfactual execution-audit framework for budgeted language-model cascades. The protocol enforces call-before-read semantics, binds successful reads to service and cache identities, records availability and component-wise budget transitions, and freezes the event trace before any target or task scorer is joined. The central object is aggregate-equivalent trace validity: two executions can share a final answer, declared resource projection, and service histogram while differing in whether their routing decisions used only legitimately observable information. We complement single-trace invariants with counterfactual prefix non-interference (CPNI), which couples a visible prefix and policy randomness while changing only a declared hidden family. The counterfactual influence frontier (CIF) localizes the earliest violating prefix and a minimal hidden witness; projection-preserving adversarial mutation (PPAM) searches for invalid traces that remain acceptable to a non-counterfactual checker. Across frozen-cache, independently generated, and serving evaluations, the two-layer audit reports a clean false-positive rate of 0.0000, detects 0.9983 of serialized faults and 0.9982 of unlogged hidden-read faults, and changes 0.3403 of corrupted quality-resource conclusions after deterministic recomputation. The online recorder and offline CPNI audit have separate overhead measurements. Learned routing and semantic verification provide downstream compatibility studies under the same execution contract.

item.title: Foundations of Hardware-Software Leakage Contracts
item.description: arXiv:2610.20754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microarchitectural attacks such as Spectre and Meltdown undermine security by exploiting software-visible side effects of microarchitectural optimizations like caches and speculative execution. To use modern hardware securely, programmers must take into account the security implications of these optimizations. Yet instruction set architectures (ISAs)---the conventional abstraction layer between hardware and software---are ill-suited for secure programming: by design, they abstract from microarchitectural details and therefore fail to reflect their security consequences. A new security abstraction is emerging to fill this void: hardware-software leakage contracts. To support the principled development of secure software on modern hardware such contracts characterize side-channel leakage at the ISA level. Thereby they enable programmers and compilers to generate code that is provably resistant to side-channel attacks---without having to explicitly reason about the microarchitecture. On the other hand, they provide a specification for hardware designers to ensure that microarchitectures do not introduce unintended and undocumented side channels. This paper introduces the foundations of this emerging topic, discussing recent contributions and unresolved challenges along the way.

item.title: INFUSE: A Unified Surface Benchmark for Indirect Prompt Injection in Agentic Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.20776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly execute long-horizon, end-to-end workflows involving shell commands, code modification, dependency installation, and interaction with remote services. This growing autonomy expands their exposure to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in external content are interpreted as legitimate task directives. Existing evaluations, however, often focus on isolated malicious strings, single-step tool calls, or narrowly scoped agent configurations. We introduce INFUSE, an end-to-end benchmark for evaluating IPI throughout the lifecycle of long-horizon agent workflows. INFUSE comprises 40 realistic tasks and a structured taxonomy of 56 attack scenarios spanning five threat categories. Attacks are injected through realistic interaction surfaces encountered during task execution, extending evaluation beyond attacks placed only in initial prompts or isolated tool interactions. We evaluate 19 LLMs from the GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, producing 41,824 adversarial trajectories (26,220 without defenses) and 720 benign reference runs. Across the benchmark, mean attack success reaches 19.6% under LLM-based evaluation and 15.4% under heuristic verification, with per-model ASR-L ranging from 3.2% to 41.9%. Existing guard models provide limited protection, while prompt-level instructional hardening reduces mean attack success from 58.2% to 14.3%, revealing substantial but model-dependent security-utility trade-offs. Our code is available at https://github.com/judydnguyen/infuse.

item.title: Privacy-Preserving Text Inference for Health-Misinformation Classification and Semantic Retrieval
item.description: arXiv:2610.20796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Health-misinformation analysis presents a dual challenge: misleading claims can affect public well-being, while systems designed to detect them may expose sensitive user-submitted text. This motivates privacy-preserving inference for public-health applications in which user queries may contain confidential medical information and trained models and reference databases are maintained on organizational servers. We design a privacy-preserving text inference framework based on CKKS homomorphic encryption for health-misinformation classification and semantic retrieval. The classification pipeline fuses BioBERT embeddings, PCA-reduced MPNet embeddings, and SVD-reduced TF-IDF features, while the retrieval pipeline combines MPNet embeddings with ISCC-SCT semantic fingerprints through late fusion. We evaluate predictive performance and benchmark plaintext versus ciphertext-based execution. The hybrid classifier achieved an accuracy of 0.971 and a macro-F1 score of 0.950, with identical reported metrics under plaintext and ciphertext-based inference. The hybrid late-fusion similarity model achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.8691 with human sentence-pair similarity scores on STS-B. For ciphertext-based retrieval, we evaluated naive and optimized implementations. The optimized implementation uses CKKS single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) packing to compute and return multiple similarity scores together, reducing single-query latency over 7,128 indexed items from 222.028 to 5.168 seconds and communication overhead from 6.11 GB to 2.13 MB. These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of privacy-preserving text inference for health-misinformation applications and characterize its predictive utility and efficiency trade-offs.

item.title: Performance Characterization of Pulsar's Software-defined Watermark Verifier
item.description: arXiv:2610.20827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pulsar provides the world's most secure PNT service by incorporating a Combinatorial Watermark into its ranging service. Under conservative signal conditions, Pulsar's Combinatorial Watermark, where 21 ranging code chips are inverted among the 1023, provides 32-bit authentication security each second. In this work, we present our software-defined radio (SDR) implementation of the Pulsar watermark processor. We discuss various threat models, multiple receiver architectures, implications to the receiver, and results from using Pulsar's SDR processing watermarked signals daily from the Pulsar-0 mission. Our results demonstrate the feasible implementation of Pulsar's watermark verification process in commercial GNSS receivers. This is an important milestone in making Xona's Pulsar service available to customers later this year after deployment of our first four production satellites.

item.title: GhostLock: Learning-Assisted Blind GPS Signal Nullification Without Victim-Side Information
item.description: arXiv:2610.20831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Global Positioning System (GPS) provides critical positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services for numerous safety- and mission-critical applications, making it an attractive target for physical-layer attacks. While GPS spoofing and jamming have been extensively studied, GPS Signal Nullification (GSN)-a physical-layer attack that suppresses authentic satellite signals through destructive interference prior to acquisition-remains largely unexplored. Existing wireless signal nullification techniques target conventional communication systems and typically require victim-side information, such as channel estimates or synchronization parameters, making them impractical for GPS. Furthermore, many GPS spoofing defenses assume authentic satellite signals remain available as trusted references, an assumption invalidated by GSN. To address this gap, we present GhostLock, a learning-assisted blind GSN framework requiring only an approximate target location estimate. GhostLock integrates a Blind Adaptive Filter (BAF) with a deep learning-based synchronization module to generate and align an anti-signal using only the attacker's locally received GPS signal, eliminating the need for victim-side observations. We implement GhostLock on a real-time software-defined radio (SDR) platform using GPS-SDR-SIM and GNU Radio. Experimental results demonstrate successful suppression of GPS signal acquisition, establishing the feasibility of blind GSN and motivating new detection and mitigation techniques for this emerging GPS threat model.

item.title: Thinking in Graphs: Neo4j-Backed Exploit-Chain Reasoning for LLM Penetration-Testing Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.20902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can drive penetration-testing tools, but they reason about an engagement as a flat list of findings in a context window. Attackers think in graphs: isolated low-severity exposures turn catastrophic once chained through credential capture, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This gap feeds a common belief that AI agents cannot truly chain exploitation; we argue this describes the flat context window, not the model. We present ChainGraph, a pattern that externalizes exploit-chain reasoning into a Neo4j property graph wired to an off-the-shelf agent via the Model Context Protocol, no bespoke harness. Findings, attack steps, credentials, assets, and tamper-evident evidence receipts are typed nodes with pre/post-condition edges; JSON/Markdown holds documentary memory while Neo4j holds reasoning memory.
